description: From Egypt to China, the bird that rises from its ashes crosses civilizations. The same dream: that the destruction will never be definitive.

hero.hook: A bird dies in the fire and returns. Why have so many cultures invented the same dream?

blocks.text: The **Phoenix** is the firebird that is reborn from its own ashes. More than a creature from a story, he carries a human dream: **resurrection**, renewal, the triumph of life over death.
From the Nile valley to the palaces of China, the figure changes shape. But the idea remains: what burns can start again. This is how the myth travels, from ancient Egypt to our rebuilt cities.
The ancestor of the Phoenix is ​​Egyptian: the **Bénou**. Its name comes from a verb meaning “to shine” or “to rise.” It was often represented as a heron, not as a flaming bird of prey.

blocks.caption: The Benu, sacred heron linked to the sun and creation.

blocks.text: According to the priests of , city of solar worship, Benu was the first living being on **Pierre Benben**, a hill emerging from liquid chaos. His cry opened time. Linked to the sun god **D**, then to **Osiris**, god of the dead, he promised the cycle: the sun dies every evening and is reborn every morning. [[Heliopolis]]
The gray heron, probable model of Benu, often stands still facing the rising sun. The Egyptians saw it as a gesture of solar worship.

The Greek historian **Herodotus** transformed the Benu into **Phoenix**: a rare bird with red and golden feathers, which returns every **500 years**. The Romans, including the poet **Ovid** and the naturalist **Pliny the Elder**, set the spectacular ending.

blocks.caption: The Phoenix ignites: destruction and rebirth in a single gesture.

blocks.text: The Phoenix is ​​unique. When it weakens, it builds a nest of spices, cinnamon, myrrh, spikenard. The sun or the beating of its wings sets fire. From the ashes a young bird is born. He carries the remains of his eldest to the altar of the sun in Egypt.
For Rome, the bird became a symbol of the **Aeternitas**, the eternity of the Empire. Later, Christians would read the image of the resurrection there.

sections.title: The Greeks and Romans invented the stake

blocks.text: In China,  is not really a burning bird. She is a creature of harmony, often linked to the **empress**. Its appearance announces a just sovereign or an era of peace. [[The Chinese Fenghuang]]

blocks.caption: Fenghuang: omen of peace and imperial symbol.

blocks.text: In Japan, **Hōō** plays a similar role. We see it on the roofs of temples in , and on **10,000 yen notes**. Here, the bird speaks less of survival after death than of moral and cosmic balance. [[Kyoto]]

sections.title: In Asia, another bird of virtue

blocks.text: In the Middle Ages, alchemists made the Phoenix a metaphor. The  of metals, and especially the dark phase called , recalls its cycle: it is necessary to destroy in order to purify. The  becomes the image of the reborn spirit. [[transmutation]] [[nigredo]] [[The Phoenix in medieval alchemy]]
The town of **Phoenix**, in Arizona, was named in **1867**: it stood on the canals and ruins of the Hohokam civilization, which had disappeared centuries earlier.
Other cousin birds populate the world: the Persian **Simorgh**, the **Anqa** of Islamic traditions. Everywhere, the same need: to believe that destruction is not definitive.

From the Egyptian **Bénou** to the Greco-Roman Phoenix and the Asian **Fenghuang**, the bird of renewal connects sun, fire and immortality. A universal myth to say that we can be reborn after the fire.
